lessons.title: Homeostasis
lessons.summary: Understand why the body must keep its internal conditions steady, how receptors, coordination centres and effectors work together, and how negative feedback keeps everything in range.
objectives: I can define homeostasis and explain why it is important for enzyme action and cell function.
I can name the conditions controlled in the human body, including blood glucose, body temperature and water levels.
I can describe the roles of receptors, coordination centres and effectors in an automatic control system.
I can explain how negative feedback returns a condition to its optimum level.

activities.title: Keeping conditions steady
activities.content:
## What is homeostasis?

**Homeostasis** is the regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function, in response to internal and external changes.

That is the exam definition. In plainer words: your body keeps its inside conditions **steady** even when the outside world, or your own activity, changes.

### Why does it matter?

The cells of your body run on **enzymes**, and enzymes only work well within a narrow range of temperature and pH. Cells also need the right amount of water and glucose:

- Too hot and enzymes **denature**; too cold and reactions slow down.
- Too little glucose and cells cannot respire enough to release energy; too much and water moves out of cells by osmosis.
- Too little water and cells shrink; too much and they swell and may burst.

### What is controlled in humans?

Three conditions you must know:

1. **Blood glucose concentration**
2. **Body temperature** (about 37 °C)
3. **Water levels** in the blood and cells

These systems are **automatic**: you do not have to think about them. Some responses involve **nerves** (fast, electrical) and others involve **hormones** (slower, chemical, carried in the blood).

question.text: Which of the following are conditions controlled by homeostasis in the human body? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Think about what enzymes and cells need to be kept constant.
question.explanation: Body temperature and blood glucose concentration are both controlled by homeostasis, along with water levels. Height and hair colour are not regulated conditions.

options.text: Body temperature
Blood glucose concentration
Height
options.feedback: Height is determined by growth and genes, not regulated minute by minute.

options.text: Hair colour

activities.title: The three parts of a control system
activities.content:
## Receptors, coordination centres and effectors

Every automatic control system, whether it uses nerves or hormones, has the same three parts:

| Part | Job | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Receptor** | Cells that **detect** a stimulus (a change in the environment, inside or outside the body) | Temperature receptors in the skin; cells in the pancreas that detect glucose; light receptors in the eye |
| **Coordination centre** | **Receives and processes** information from the receptors and decides what response is needed | The **brain**, the **spinal cord** and the **pancreas** |
| **Effector** | **Brings about the response** that restores the optimum level | **Muscles** (which contract) and **glands** (which secrete substances such as hormones or sweat) |

The flow of information is always:

```
stimulus -> receptor -> coordination centre -> effector -> response
```

**Tip:** the two types of effector are *muscles* and *glands*. Muscles respond by contracting; glands respond by secreting.

A receptor on its own cannot fix anything, and an effector on its own does not know when to act. It is the coordination centre that links the two, which is why the brain, spinal cord and pancreas are so important.

activities.title: Worked example: identifying the parts
activities.content:
**On a cold day you start to shiver. Identify the stimulus, receptor, coordination centre, effector and response.**

| Part | In this example |
|---|---|
| Stimulus | A fall in body or skin temperature |
| Receptor | Temperature receptors in the skin and in the brain |
| Coordination centre | The brain (specifically its thermoregulatory centre) |
| Effector | Skeletal muscles |
| Response | Muscles contract rapidly (shivering), releasing heat from respiration |

**Now a hormonal example. After a sugary drink, blood glucose rises and the pancreas releases insulin.**

| Part | In this example |
|---|---|
| Stimulus | Rise in blood glucose concentration |
| Receptor | Cells in the pancreas that detect glucose |
| Coordination centre | The pancreas |
| Effector | Cells in the liver and muscles (which take up glucose) and the pancreas gland that secretes insulin |
| Response | Glucose removed from the blood and stored as glycogen |

Notice that in the second example the pancreas acts as both receptor and coordination centre.

question.text: Put the parts of a control system in the order that information flows through them.
question.hint: Something changes, something notices, something decides, something acts.
question.explanation: Stimulus → receptor → coordination centre → effector → response.

question.text: Match each structure to its role in a control system.
question.hint: Which one detects, which one decides, and which one acts?
question.explanation: Temperature receptors in the skin detect changes; the brain is a coordination centre; a sweat gland is an effector.

activities.title: Negative feedback
activities.content:
## Bringing things back to normal

Most homeostatic systems use **negative feedback**. The idea is simple: when a condition moves *away* from its optimum, the body triggers a response that moves it *back* the other way. Once the level returns to normal, the response switches off.

```
  level rises above optimum
            |
   receptor detects rise
            |
   coordination centre
            |
   effector acts to LOWER the level
            |
   level returns to optimum -> response stops
```

The same happens in reverse if the level falls too low: the effector acts to **raise** it.

It is called *negative* feedback because the response always **opposes** the change. The result is that the condition does not stay perfectly fixed but **oscillates** slightly around the optimum, a little above, then a little below.

### Examples

- **Temperature**: too hot → sweating and vasodilation lose heat → temperature falls. Too cold → shivering and vasoconstriction conserve heat → temperature rises.
- **Blood glucose**: too high → insulin released → glucose stored → level falls. Too low → glucagon released → glycogen converted to glucose → level rises.

When describing negative feedback in an exam, always finish with the level returning to normal and the response stopping.

activities.title: Worked example: writing a negative feedback answer
activities.content:
**Question: A person drinks a large volume of water. Explain, using the idea of negative feedback, how their body responds. (3 marks)**

**Step-by-step model answer:**

1. **Change detected:** *"The water content of the blood rises above the optimum, and this is detected by receptors in the brain."*
2. **Response opposes the change:** *"The brain causes the kidneys to remove more water from the blood, so a larger volume of dilute urine is produced."*
3. **Return to normal:** *"The water content of the blood falls back to the optimum, and the response then stops."*

**Why this scores full marks:**

- It names the change and the receptor.
- It describes a response that goes in the *opposite* direction to the change.
- It states that the level returns to normal, which is the defining feature of negative feedback.

**Common mistake:** describing only the change and the response, without saying that the response reverses the change. Without that link the answer describes a reaction, not negative feedback.

question.text: Which statement best describes negative feedback?
question.hint: Think about the direction of the response compared with the original change.
question.explanation: In negative feedback the response reverses the change, bringing the condition back towards its optimum. The response stops once the level is normal.

options.text: A change is detected and a response is triggered that reverses the change
A change is detected and a response is triggered that increases the change
options.feedback: That would be positive feedback, which is rare in homeostasis.

options.text: A condition is kept exactly constant with no variation
options.feedback: Levels oscillate slightly around the optimum.

options.text: The body ignores small changes and only responds to large ones

metadata.blanksText: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions at their ___ level. A ___ detects a change, and an ___ such as a muscle or gland brings about the response.

question.hint: The first word means 'best'; the other two are the first and last parts of a control system.
question.explanation: Homeostasis maintains optimum conditions. Receptors detect stimuli and effectors (muscles or glands) carry out responses.

question.text:
During exercise, a runner's body temperature starts to rise.

(a) Explain why it is important that body temperature does not rise too far. (2 marks)

(b) Describe how the body responds to the rise in temperature. In your answer identify the receptor, coordination centre and an effector, and explain how this is an example of negative feedback. (3 marks)
question.hint: For (a), think about enzymes. For (b), the response must lower the temperature and stop when it is back to normal.
question.explanation: (a) Enzymes control the reactions in cells and work best at about 37 °C. If the temperature rises too far the enzymes denature (their active site changes shape) and reactions such as respiration stop. (b) Temperature receptors in the skin and brain detect the rise. The thermoregulatory centre in the brain processes this and sends impulses to effectors: sweat glands release sweat which evaporates and cools the skin, and blood vessels near the skin surface dilate so more heat is lost. This is negative feedback because the response lowers the temperature, reversing the original change, and stops once the temperature is back to normal.

markScheme.criterion: Enzymes work best at optimum temperature / around 37 °C
High temperature denatures enzymes so reactions stop / slow
Receptor (skin/brain temperature receptors) and coordination centre (brain / thermoregulatory centre) identified
Effector and response: sweat glands produce sweat / blood vessels dilate, so heat is lost
Negative feedback: response reverses the change and stops when temperature returns to normal

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Homeostasis** = regulating internal conditions to maintain optimum conditions for function, in response to internal and external changes.
- It matters because **enzymes** and cells need the right temperature, pH, glucose and water levels.
- Humans control **blood glucose**, **body temperature** and **water levels**.
- Control systems: **receptor** (detects) → **coordination centre** (brain, spinal cord, pancreas) → **effector** (muscle or gland) → response.
- **Negative feedback**: the response opposes the change and stops once the level is back at the optimum, so levels oscillate slightly around normal.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: homeostasis only involves the nervous system.
practiceQuestions.hint: Insulin is a hormone, and it helps control blood glucose.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Homeostasis can involve nervous responses (fast, electrical) or chemical responses using hormones.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these is an effector?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Muscles and glands are effectors. The others detect or coordinate.

options.text: A muscle
A light receptor in the eye
The spinal cord
A temperature receptor in the skin

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following can act as coordination centres in the human body? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: There are three named in the specification.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The brain, spinal cord and pancreas are coordination centres. The skin contains receptors and the liver acts as an effector for blood glucose control.

options.text: Brain
Pancreas
Skin
options.feedback: The skin contains receptors and effectors, but does not coordinate.

options.text: Liver

metadata.blanksText: Homeostasis is the regulation of the ___ conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function, in response to internal and ___ changes.

practiceQuestions.hint: The first blank is the opposite of 'external'; the second is the opposite of 'internal'.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Homeostasis regulates internal conditions in response to internal and external changes.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why body temperature is kept close to 37 °C.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the molecules that control reactions in cells.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Enzymes that control reactions in the body work best at about 37 °C. If the temperature is too high they denature, and if it is too low reactions slow down.

markScheme.criterion: Enzymes have an optimum temperature of about 37 °C
Too hot causes denaturing / too cold slows reactions

practiceQuestions.text: Match each change to the negative feedback response that corrects it.
practiceQuestions.hint: Each response works in the opposite direction to the change.
practiceQuestions.explanation: High blood glucose triggers insulin release; low body temperature triggers shivering; high blood water content leads to more dilute urine.

pairs.left: Water content of blood rises too high
pairs.right: Kidneys produce a larger volume of dilute urine

practiceQuestions.text: Put these events in order to describe negative feedback when blood glucose rises after a meal.
practiceQuestions.hint: Detection comes before the hormone; the hormone comes before storage.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Blood glucose rises → pancreas detects it → insulin released → liver and muscles take up glucose → blood glucose falls back to normal.
order: Blood glucose concentration rises above normal
Cells in the pancreas detect the rise
The pancreas releases insulin into the blood
Liver and muscle cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen
Blood glucose returns to normal and insulin release falls

practiceQuestions.text:
A student says: "Homeostasis keeps body temperature at exactly 37.0 °C at all times."

(a) Explain why the student's statement is not quite correct, using the idea of negative feedback. (2 marks)

(b) A person steps out of a warm house into snow. Identify the receptor, coordination centre and one effector involved in the body's response. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: In (a), think about what happens between the change being detected and the response taking effect. Does the level ever stop moving?
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Negative feedback only acts once a change has been detected, so temperature rises or falls slightly before the response brings it back. The temperature therefore oscillates around 37 °C rather than staying exactly fixed. (b) Receptor: temperature receptors in the skin. Coordination centre: the brain (thermoregulatory centre). Effector: skeletal muscles that shiver, or blood vessels in the skin that constrict, or hair erector muscles.

markScheme.criterion: Response only happens after a change is detected, so the level moves away from 37 °C first
Temperature fluctuates / oscillates around 37 °C rather than staying exactly constant
Receptor in skin and coordination centre brain identified
Effector identified: muscles (shivering), blood vessels (constrict) or hair erector muscles

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these is a difference between nervous and hormonal control?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about speed and how the signal travels.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Nervous responses use electrical impulses along neurones and are fast; hormonal responses use chemicals carried in the blood and are slower but longer-lasting.

options.text: Nervous responses are faster and use electrical impulses; hormonal responses use chemicals in the blood
Nervous responses use chemicals in the blood; hormonal responses use electrical impulses
Only nervous responses are involved in homeostasis
Hormonal responses are always faster than nervous responses
options.feedback: Hormones travel in the blood, so they act more slowly.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a gland can be an effector.
practiceQuestions.hint: What are the two types of effector?
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Effectors are muscles, which contract, or glands, which secrete substances such as hormones or sweat.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following are examples of homeostasis? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Homeostasis keeps an internal condition steady; growth and protective reflexes do not.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sweating to bring a rising body temperature back down and releasing insulin to bring a rising blood glucose level back down both keep internal conditions steady, so they are homeostasis. Blinking is a protective reflex and growing taller is development, not the regulation of a condition.

options.text: Sweating when body temperature starts to rise
Releasing insulin when blood glucose rises after a meal
Blinking when an object comes close to the eye
options.feedback: Blinking is a protective reflex; it does not keep an internal condition constant.

options.text: Growing taller during puberty
options.feedback: Growth is not the regulation of an internal condition.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these events in order to describe what happens when a person walks into a very cold room.
practiceQuestions.hint: Follow the flow: change, detection, processing, action, result.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Body temperature starts to fall (stimulus) → temperature receptors in the skin detect the change → the thermoregulatory centre in the brain processes the information → muscles shiver and skin blood vessels narrow (effectors) → body temperature returns to normal.
order: Temperature receptors in the skin detect the change
The thermoregulatory centre in the brain processes the information
Muscles shiver and blood vessels in the skin narrow

practiceQuestions.text: Match each structure to the part it plays in a control system.
practiceQuestions.hint: Detecting, processing and acting are three different jobs.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Light receptor cells in the eye detect a stimulus, so they are receptors; the spinal cord processes information, so it is a coordination centre; a salivary gland produces a response, so it is an effector.

pairs.left: Light receptor cell in the eye

practiceQuestions.text: After a person drinks a large glass of water, the water content of their blood rises. The kidneys respond by producing a larger volume of dilute urine until the water content is back to normal. Why is this an example of negative feedback?
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the direction of the response with the direction of the original change.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The original change was a rise in water content; the response (losing more water in urine) reverses that change and stops once the level is back to normal. A response that reverses a change is negative feedback.

options.text: The response reverses the original change and stops when the level is back to normal
The response makes the water content of the blood rise even further
options.feedback: That would be positive feedback, which does not restore a steady level.

options.text: The response happens without the person being aware of it
options.feedback: Many responses are unconscious; that is not what defines negative feedback.

options.text: The kidneys always produce the same volume of urine whatever happens

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the passage about control systems.

metadata.blanksText: The change that a control system responds to is called a ___. Coordination centres such as the brain, spinal cord and ___ receive and process information from receptors. Effectors then bring about a ___ that restores the optimum level.

practiceQuestions.hint: The first word is what a receptor detects; the second is an organ that controls blood glucose; the third is what an effector produces.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A stimulus is detected by receptors. The brain, spinal cord and pancreas act as coordination centres. Effectors (muscles or glands) produce a response.

practiceQuestions.text:
A swimmer climbs out of a cold lake on a windy day and her body temperature starts to fall.

(a) Explain why it is important that body temperature does not fall too far. (2 marks)

(b) Describe how the body responds to the fall in temperature. In your answer identify the receptor, coordination centre and an effector, and explain how this is an example of negative feedback. (3 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a), think about the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions in the cold. For (b), the response must raise the temperature and stop once it is back to normal.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Enzymes control the reactions in cells and work best at about 37 °C. If the temperature falls too far the enzymes work much more slowly, so reactions such as respiration are too slow to release the energy the cells need. (b) Temperature receptors in the skin detect the fall. The thermoregulatory centre in the brain processes this and sends impulses to effectors: skeletal muscles shiver, which releases heat from respiration, and blood vessels near the skin surface constrict so less heat is lost from the skin. This is negative feedback because the response raises the temperature, reversing the original change, and stops once the temperature is back to normal.

markScheme.criterion: Enzymes work best at optimum temperature / around 37 °C
Low temperature slows enzyme activity so reactions (e.g. respiration) are too slow
Receptor (skin temperature receptors) and coordination centre (brain / thermoregulatory centre) identified
Effector and response: muscles shiver / blood vessels constrict, so heat is generated or less heat is lost
Negative feedback: response reverses the change and stops when temperature returns to normal
